title: Simple Views
description: Build SQL simple views with explicit columns, live base-table reads, NULL and duplicate rules, check options, and safe employee reporting exercises.

questions.question_text: What defines a 'simple view' as opposed to a 'complex view'?
options: It uses fewer than 100 rows
It is based on a single table with no joins, aggregation, GROUP BY, or DISTINCT
It is read-only
It has no WHERE clause
questions.explanation: A simple view draws from one base table and performs no joins, aggregation, GROUP BY, or DISTINCT — essentially a filtered/projected view of one table.

questions.question_text: When you run `SELECT * FROM high_earners`, where does the data actually come from?
options: A cached copy stored inside the view
The underlying employees table, queried fresh at that moment
A snapshot taken when the view was created
The database's system catalog
questions.explanation: A plain (non-materialized) view has no storage of its own; it re-runs its defining query against the base table each time it is queried.

questions.question_text: Given `CREATE VIEW high_earners AS SELECT id, name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 80000; `, what happens if an employee's salary is updated through the view from 85000 down to 70000?
options: The update is rejected outright
The row disappears from subsequent queries on the view because it no longer matches the WHERE clause
The view definition is automatically changed
The underlying table is unaffected
questions.explanation: Since the row no longer satisfies salary > 80000, it will no longer appear when the view is queried again — unless WITH CHECK OPTION is used to prevent such updates.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a valid simple view definition?
options: CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT department, AVG(salary) FROM employees GROUP BY department;
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT e.name, d.name FROM employees e JOIN departments d ON e.department = d.id;
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT id, name, department FROM employees;
CREATE VIEW v AS SELECT DISTINCT department FROM employees;
questions.explanation: This is a single-table projection with no joins, aggregation, GROUP BY, or DISTINCT — the hallmark of a simple view. The others involve GROUP BY, a JOIN, or DISTINCT, making them complex views.

questions.question_text: Why might a team create `employee_directory AS SELECT id, name, department FROM employees` instead of letting everyone query employees directly?
options: Views run faster than tables in every case
To hide the salary column from users who only need directory information
Views are required by SQL syntax rules
It reduces the number of rows in the employees table
questions.explanation: Restricting the column list in a view is a common technique to expose only non-sensitive columns to a broader audience — an early example of view-based security (Chapter 19.4).

questions.question_text: If the employees table gains a new column `bonus` after `high_earners` (defined with an explicit column list, not SELECT *) was created, what happens?
options: high_earners immediately shows the new bonus column
high_earners still only returns id, name, salary since its column list is fixed
The view is automatically dropped
An error occurs the next time the view is queried
questions.explanation: Extending the exposed output requires a deliberate change to the view definition, such as ALTER VIEW or CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW in MySQL. Adding a base-table column does not automatically extend this explicit projection.

questions.question_text: Can two views in the same schema share the same name?
options: Yes, as long as their definitions differ
No — a view name must be unique among tables and views in that schema
Yes, if one is simple and the other complex
Only in materialized views
questions.explanation: A view occupies the same namespace as tables in its schema, so its name must be unique among both tables and views.

questions.question_text: In terms of query execution, what typically happens to `SELECT * FROM high_earners ORDER BY salary DESC` under the hood?
options: The optimizer materializes the view permanently the first time it runs
The optimizer typically inlines/expands the view definition into the outer query and optimizes as one query
It always creates a temporary table
It bypasses the query optimizer entirely
questions.explanation: Most relational optimizers merge (inline) a non-materialized view's defining query into the outer query for planning purposes, rather than executing it as a separate, opaque step.

questions.question_text: What does an ordinary simple view persist?
options: A query definition
A permanently frozen result
A duplicate employee table
An execution plan that never changes
questions.explanation: Its result is evaluated from the underlying data rather than separately refreshed storage.

questions.question_text: Why project explicit columns in a view contract?
options: To grant every permission
To make the exposed interface deliberate
To remove all NULL values
To guarantee an index scan
questions.explanation: Explicit columns make the data contract clear.

questions.question_text: A salary is exactly 80000. Does salary > 80000 include it?
options: Yes always
No
Only if the name is unique
Only under ORDER BY
questions.explanation: The strict inequality excludes the boundary value.

questions.question_text: What happens after a committed eligible employee is added to the base table?
options: The view must always be rebuilt
A trigger must copy the row first
An eligible fresh read can include the employee
The view becomes invalid automatically
questions.explanation: Ordinary views evaluate the base data under transaction visibility rules.

questions.question_text: Can a view exposing only id and name be queried for salary?
options: Yes because all table columns are implicit
Yes only with DISTINCT
Yes only with ORDER BY
No, salary is outside its columns
questions.explanation: The visible columns define the query interface.

questions.question_text: Which condition admits a row with NULL salary?
options: salary IS NULL
salary = NULL
salary > 80000
salary <> NULL
questions.explanation: IS NULL explicitly tests missing values.

questions.question_text: What does WITH CHECK OPTION control?
options: All direct writes to every base table
Eligible writes through the view must satisfy its condition
Every SELECT order
Automatic salary defaults
questions.explanation: The check applies to the view write path.

questions.question_text: Why can inserting through high_earners fail when department is omitted?
options: Every view is always read only
A salary filter forbids all names
A required base column may lack a value or default
ORDER BY is absent
questions.explanation: Insertability depends on base requirements as well as the view shape.

questions.question_text: Does a view automatically remove equal projected names?
options: Yes always
Only for text
Only for primary key tables
No, unless the query requests deduplication
questions.explanation: Ordinary projections preserve row occurrences.

questions.question_text: Where should a consumer specify guaranteed report order?
options: Its final SELECT ORDER BY
Only in insertion order
In a column alias
In the view name
questions.explanation: Consumers should explicitly order their result.

questions.question_text: What should be inspected before renaming a view column?
options: Only the table row count
Direct callers and dependent definitions
Only the database size
Only duplicate names
questions.explanation: Column names are part of the caller contract.

questions.question_text: Does creating a view alone prove a security boundary?
options: Yes, all base access is revoked
Yes, every view enforces row isolation
No, roles and underlying privilege behavior must be reviewed
Yes, hidden columns are deleted
questions.explanation: Visibility and authorization require separate trusted enforcement.

coding_problems.title: Create a High Earners View

original_problem.title: Create a High Earners View
original_problem.description:
Write a `CREATE VIEW` statement named `high_earners` that exposes `id`, `name`, `salary` for every employee earning more than 80000. The checker will query your view afterward.

```sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  name TEXT NOT NULL,
  department TEXT NOT NULL,
  salary INTEGER NOT NULL
);
```

**Sample data**:

```sql
INSERT INTO employees (id, name, department, salary) VALUES
(1, 'Asha', 'Engineering', 90000),
(2, 'Rohan', 'Engineering', 60000),
(3, 'Neha', 'Sales', 70000),
(4, 'Vikram', 'Sales', 50000);
```

notes:
## Give a useful query a stable name

A finance assistant repeatedly needs employee identifiers, names, and salaries above a threshold. Copying the same SELECT into five reports invites inconsistent edits. A simple view gives that query a database name. Readers query the name as though it were a table, while the database evaluates the stored definition against its underlying data. The ordinary view stores a query definition rather than a separately refreshed result set. It is a reusable interface over data, not an independent copy of employees.

In introductory teaching, a simple view usually means a projection and optional filter over one base table, without grouping, aggregates, or set operations. This description is a useful learning category rather than a universal SQL keyword. The exact operations permitted through a view depend on its definition and the database engine. Begin by understanding the selected rows and columns; then separately consider update capability, permissions, and execution cost.

## Define and read the interface

The example uses MySQL syntax and integer salary units for a compact fixture. The department column remains in the table but is intentionally omitted from the view. An explicit column list makes this interface easy to review and prevents a newly added base column from accidentally becoming part of a reporting contract.

```sql
CREATE TABLE employees (
 id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
 name VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
 department VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
 salary INTEGER NOT NULL
);
INSERT INTO employees VALUES
 (1,'Asha','Engineering',90000),
 (2,'Rohan','Engineering',60000),
 (3,'Neha','Sales',80000),
 (4,'Vikram','Sales',95000);
CREATE VIEW high_earners AS
SELECT id,name,salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 80000;
SELECT id,name,salary FROM high_earners ORDER BY id;
```

The expected result contains Asha with 90000 and Vikram with 95000. Neha is excluded because the predicate is strictly greater than 80000. This output follows from the fixture; it is not a claim that a database was executed here. Boundary cases belong in tests because changing greater than to greater than or equal changes the business rule without causing a syntax error.

The view exposes only three columns. A query requesting department directly from high_earners fails because department is outside that interface. Consumers needing department must use another authorized interface or a reviewed change to this view. A view can hide structural complexity, but it should not encourage callers to assume columns exist merely because they exist somewhere underneath it.

## Observe changes in the base table

After increasing Rohan's salary to 85000, a fresh query of high_earners includes Rohan. There is no manual refresh command for this ordinary view. Transaction isolation still matters: a reader sees data according to its transaction's visibility rules, rather than necessarily seeing every concurrent change immediately. A view does not replace transaction semantics.

```sql
UPDATE employees SET salary=85000 WHERE id=2;
SELECT id,name,salary FROM high_earners ORDER BY id;
```

The expected identifiers are now 1, 2, and 4. If an application continues displaying an older result, inspect its cache, transaction snapshot, connection routing, and read timing before blaming the view definition. Separately stored summaries and materialized views have different maintenance rules. Calling every cached result a view obscures the source of staleness.

## Filters, NULL, and duplicates

A WHERE predicate admits rows for which the condition is true. If salary were nullable, a missing salary would not pass salary > 80000, because that comparison is unknown. COALESCE can assign an explicit fallback but should follow a business decision. A missing salary is not automatically equivalent to a real zero salary. In this fixture NOT NULL prevents that ambiguity at the base table boundary.

A view does not remove duplicates unless its SELECT requests that behavior. Two employees named Asha can both appear when they have distinct identifiers. If the view exposes only name, the display may show the same name twice. Adding DISTINCT changes the result and can affect update capability. Keep an identifying column when a consumer must distinguish employees rather than merely list distinct labels.

An ordinary view does not guarantee a display order. Even if a definition includes ordering syntax accepted by the engine, a consumer should specify its own final ORDER BY. Sorting by salary alone leaves ties unordered. Add id as a tie breaker for predictable pagination and comparison. A stable interface describes both the row grain and the columns, while each consuming report specifies its presentation order.

## Writing through a simple view

Some simple views allow UPDATE or DELETE to affect the corresponding base rows. That does not mean every possible insert succeeds. Required base columns omitted from the view may prevent insertion when they have no default. In this example department is required and absent, so an insert providing only the visible columns cannot supply a valid employee. Prefer an explicit write interface when callers need more information than a reporting view exposes.

A filter alone does not necessarily prevent a permitted update from making a row disappear from the view. If Asha's salary is changed to 70000 through an updatable filtered view, the row can leave its result unless the definition includes the appropriate check option. WITH CHECK OPTION requires writes made through that view to satisfy its selection condition. It does not validate unrelated business rules or protect writes performed directly against the base table.

```sql
CREATE VIEW checked_high_earners AS
SELECT id,name,salary FROM employees WHERE salary > 80000
WITH CHECK OPTION;
```

A permitted salary update below the threshold through checked_high_earners is rejected. This is a local rule for that view path. Base constraints and trusted authorization still carry responsibility for the entire database. Do not infer that creating a view has granted access or revoked existing table privileges.

## Worked lab: add an active staff interface

Suppose an employees table also has active as a nonnullable integer flag. The task is to expose id and name only for active employees, while keeping salary private from this interface. Define active_staff using an explicit projection and WHERE active = 1, then select id and name ordered by id. With rows Asha active and Rohan inactive, only Asha appears. Make Rohan active and the next eligible read includes him.

The solution is simple because the rule is simple. Do not duplicate the active flag in a second table or schedule a copy operation. Test zero active staff, multiple staff with the same name, and changes from active to inactive. If the interface is expected to support writes, review the omitted required columns and check option separately. Read correctness does not prove insertability.

## Worked lab: extend a report safely

A second task asks for high earners in Engineering. Query the existing view and join an authorized department interface by employee id, or define a separate purpose specific view over the base table. Avoid changing the existing view's threshold merely to satisfy this one report. Other callers may rely on the original meaning. Use an explicit new name when a different business meaning deserves a separate contract.

Inspect dependencies before changing or replacing a view. A renamed output column can break queries even when the base table remains untouched. Record the previous definition, compare representative results, and check denied access with the intended database roles in a separately authorized environment. Creating a view in a lesson is a design illustration, not permission to run production DDL.

## Names and expression columns

Expressions need meaningful aliases when exposed as view columns. A derived annual estimate, for example, should say which salary unit it assumes and whether rounding applies. A computed column can be useful to readers even if it cannot be assigned directly during an update. Keep these two questions separate: can the database evaluate the expression, and can a write be mapped unambiguously back to a base column?

## Practical boundaries

A view provides reuse and a stable projection; it does not automatically accelerate the underlying query. The optimizer may merge a definition into a surrounding query or process it another way. Measure the actual consuming query if performance matters. Avoid deep chains of views that make row filters and joins difficult to trace.

Use [View Maintenance](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/view-maintenance) to distinguish ordinary definitions from stored summaries. [UNION ALL](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/union-all) explains a result combination that is useful for reporting but changes the simplicity and write behavior of a view definition.
